text:
Re Ontario Public Service Employees Union and Forer et al.

52 O.R. (2d) 705

ONTARIO

COURT OF APPEAL

BLAIR, THORSON AND CORY JJ.A.

21ST NOVEMBER 1985.

Administrative law -- Judicial review -- Privative clauses -- Statute giving administrative tribunal exclusive jurisdiction to determine questions of law or fact -- No reference to certiorari -- Standard of review whether tribunal's decision patently unreasonable -- Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 108, s. 39.
Trade unions -- Religious objection -- Jewish employee objecting to resolution of provincial labour federation urging Canadian Labour Congress to call upon Canadian Government to recognize Palestine Liberation Organization as legitimate representative of Palestinian people -- Tribunal granting employee exemption from union dues on basis of religious objection -- Tribunal's decision not patently unreasonable -- Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 108, s. 16(2).
An individual sought exemption from payment of union dues pursuant to s. 16(2) of the Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 108, on the basis of religious convictions. Specifically, he objected to a resolution passed by the Ontario Federation of Labour, of which the union representing him was a member, urging the Canadian Labour Congress to call upon the Canadian Government to endorse the Palestine Liberation Organization as legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. The C.L.C. subsequently rejected the resolution. In the employee's view, the Jewish people had a God-given right to the land of Israel. The religious exemption was granted by the Ontario Public Service Labour Relations Tribunal. Section 39 of the Act provides that the tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to exercise the powers conferred upon it by the Act and to determine all questions of fact or law and states that the decisions of the tribunal are final and binding for all purposes. An application for judicial review of the decision was granted by the Divisional Court. On appeal, held, the appeal should be allowed.
The proper standard for review, in light of the privative clause in s. 39 of the Act, is whether the decision of the tribunal interpreting the words "religious convictions or belief " is patently unreasonable. Whether certiorari is preserved by any statute depends on the proper construction of the finality or other preclusive clauses in the context of the statute as a whole, and express language is not required to remove the right to certiorari. As courts now recognize the legitimacy of administrative tribunals as an essential part of the structure of government and the legal system, they respect the intent of Legislatures to limit judicial review. The intended effect of s. 39 is that the tribunal, acting within the jurisdiction conferred upon it, should be permitted to perform its important functions free from judicial interference.
The tribunal's interpretation of s. 16(2) was not patently unreasonable. The tribunal held that the words "his religious convictions and belief " must be considered from the subjective point of view of the applicant, and the tribunal must be convinced that the applicant's views are sincerely held as religious convictions. The word "religious" does not require that the individual's beliefs be the tenets of any religious denomination, and only in rare cases will it be necessary to test an applicant's convictions against some objective definition of the word "religious". There was evidence to support the tribunal's conclusion that the employee's views were religious.

The judgment of the court was delivered by

BLAIR J.A.:-- The principal issue in this appeal is the
effect which should be given to a statutory declaration that an
administrative tribunal's decisions are "final and binding".
The appellants appeal, with leave of this Court, from the
decision of the Divisional Court (Re Ontario Public Service
Employees Union and Forer et al. (1984),
1984 CanLII 1875 (ON HCJ)
, 46 O.R. (2d) 789, 10
D.L.R. (4th) 602) quashing a decision of the Ontario Public
Service Labour Relations Tribunal (the Tribunal).

Facts and background

The appellant Chaim Forer is an employee of the Government of
Ontario and is included in a collective agreement between the
government and the respondent Ontario Public Service Employees
Union (OPSEU). The collective agreement requires all employees
covered by it to pay dues to OPSEU whether or not they are
members of OPSEU. OPSEU is a member of the Ontario Federation
of Labour (OFL) and the Canadian Labour Congress (CLC).

In November, 1982, a convention of the OFL passed a
resolution dealing with Middle East problems. The resolution
urged the CLC to call upon the Canadian Government to support
"all avenues toward lasting peace" in the region. In
particular, it called for the withdrawal of all foreign troops
from Lebanon and their replacement by a United Nations'
peacekeeping force, the recognition of Israel's right to live
within secure borders based on pre-1967 boundaries, the
recognition of the right of the Palestinian people to a secure
and independent homeland and the recognition of the Palestine
Liberation Organization (P.L.O.) as the legitimate
representative of the Palestinian people. The resolution was
framed as a recommendation to the CLC because the OFL
constitution provides that foreign policy statements must be
made by the CLC.

Forer is a member of the Lubavitch Hasidim sect of the Jewish
religion. He applied to the Tribunal for an order under s.
16(2) of the Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O.
1980, c. 108 (the Act), exempting him from the payment of dues
to OPSEU and permitting the diversion of these dues to a
charity. Section 16(2) provides:

16(2) Where the Tribunal is satisfied that an employee
because of his religious convictions or belief objects to
paying dues or contributions to an employee organization, the
Tribunal shall order that the provisions of the collective
agreement pertaining thereto do not apply to such employee
and that the employee is not required to pay dues or
contributions to the employee organization, provided that
amounts equivalent thereto are remitted by the employer to a
charitable organization mutually agreed upon by the employee
and the employee organization and failing such agreement then
to such charitable organization registered as such under Part
I of the
Income Tax Act (Canada)
as may be designated by the
Tribunal.
(Emphasis added.)

Forer stated his objections to the payment of union dues in
the following terms:

The recent resolution of the OFL (to which OPSEU belongs)
supporting the terrorist PLO in its international war against
the Jewish people is inimical to every human being in general
and to every Jew in particular, who believes in the
eternality of the Jewish people and in their God given right
to the land of Israel. It is most obnoxious that I, a
believer, should be required to pay dues to an organization
(OPSEU) whose membership in OFL contributes to OFL's
influence on public opinion in a manner contrary to my belief
and ideals.

The Tribunal gave only brief reasons for its decision that
Forer was entitled to an exemption. It stated that its decision
was made "having regard to the evidence and to the submissions
of the parties and for the reasons given in Van Harten v. Civil
Services Ass'n of Ontario (Inc.) et al., July 5, 1976,
unreported ... ". In my opinion, the tribunal in Van Harten
correctly stated the principles which should govern a decision
on an application under s. 30. The relevant part of its
decision is fully set out because it is not reported elsewhere:

The representative for Ontario Public Service Employees
Union in this case and others has asked this tribunal to
define the term "religious convictions or belief ". The task
of determining whether a person has a religious conviction or
belief can be most difficult. This tribunal must be cautious
not to put an applicant to the condition of satisfying our
individual views as to what each of us may consider to be
religious. Also we are not prepared to disqualify certain
convictions or belief as being religious in character based
upon [an] a priori basis.

Further, we do not believe that we can define the term
"religious" in a manner that will be relevant to all
future applications under this section. There are many cases
that do not require an extensive definition to arrive at a
decision, although there may be some cases where an
applicant's convictions or belief must be tested against some
objective definition. However, we determine that the term
"religious" need not be construed in the sense that it
must be a tenet of a particular religious faith or religious
institution. An applicant's religious convictions or belief
must, in the main, be considered from a subjective point of
view. While we consider religion as being subjective and
personal to the individual, we recognize that there are
peripheral situations where an applicant may attempt to use
the concept of religion to escape from the payment of dues to
OPSEU. Thus we think it relevant to examine the sincerity of
an applicant's religious convictions or belief in order to
preclude an abuse of the section. Re Civil Service Ass'n of
Ontario (Inc.) and Anderson et al. (1975),
1975 CanLII 757 (ON HCJ)
, 9 O.R. (2d) 341
(Div. Ct.); Funk and Manitoba Labour Board (1976),
1976 CanLII 1098 (MB CA)
, 66
D.L.R. (3d) 35, [1976] 3 W.W.R. 209, 76 C.L.L.C. para.
14
,006
(C.A.); Stel v. North York Civil Employees Union, Local
94, C.U.P.E. v. Corp. of Borough of North York, [1971]
O.L.R.B. Rep. 363 at p. 375.

This tribunal is also of the opinion that once it is
determined that an applicant is religious that the applicant
must also establish that the objection to paying dues or
contributions to an employee organization stems from the
applicant's religious convictions or belief. There must be
some nexus between the religious convictions or belief and
the objection. We do not have jurisdiction to grant an
exemption to those whose social principles form the basis for
the objection. Social principles do not involve religious
convictions or belief as those terms are generally
understood: see R. v. Ontario Labour Relations Board, Ex p.
Trenton Construction Workers' Ass'n, Local 52,
1963 CanLII 117 (ON HCJ)
, [1963] 2 O.R.
376, 39 D.L.R. (2d) 593, 63 C.L.L.C. para.
15
,459 at p. 655
per McRuer C.J.H.C.

Further, we do not have the authority to grant an exemption
to persons who are religious and who have social or political
views unconnected to their religion which are contrary to
those of the employee organization. There must be
relationship between the religious convictions or belief and
the objection to the payment of dues.

Further, the tribunal realizes that an applicant may arrive
at his objection in a variety of ways. We are not prepared to
question the logic as to how an applicant arrives at his
particular religious convictions or belief, nor are we
concerned with the logical analysis of a particular applicant
in relating the objection to payment of union dues to a
religious conviction or belief -- our concern is whether the
applicant holds such religious convictions or belief and
whether he personally relates such convictions or belief to
his objection.

Applying those considerations to the facts of the instant
case, it is our opinion that the applicant is a religious man
and bases his life, as best as possible, on his
interpretation of the Bible. He is a member of a particular
church and it is without doubt that he holds religious
convictions and beliefs, that he is sincere in those beliefs
and that his objection to paying his dues is related to his
religious convictions.

The majority in the Divisional Court held that the Tribunal
had erred in characterizing Forer's views as "religious
convictions". Smith J. agreed with the view expressed in Van
Harten that "religion is subjective and personal to the
person". However, he considered that the word did not have
whatever meaning an applicant might give to it. In his view,
there were objective limits to its meaning and he said at p.
797 O.R., p. 610 D.L.R.:

It seems to me that the legislator could not have intended
the word "religious" to have only the meaning fastened upon
it by the exemption seeker. If it were so, the inquiry would
be limited to a question of degree of sincerity of the person
claiming exemption, regardless of how the conviction was
characterized by any ordinary decent and reasonable member of
the community. There must be a threshold.

He then referred to the Van Harten decision and continued:

Most of what was so ably said in Van Harten, supra, is
helpful in attempting to apply a concept as ethereal as
"religious conviction" to any and perhaps most given
factual situations. That case being entirely different from
the case at hand, the chairman's entreaty to future
tribunals, as embodied in the reasons, to be cautious not to
put an applicant to the condition of satisfying "our
individual views as to what each of us may consider to be
religious", does nothing to advance the resolution of the
problem facing us.

Again we accept readily that religion is subjective and
personal to the person. We also have no doubt as to Mr.
Forer's sincerity.

The troubling feature of this case, however, lies in Mr.
Forer's expressed position that everything is religious. I
pause to say that it is common ground that Mr. Forer was the
only person to give evidence below and we had the benefit of
his statement and submissions when he appeared before us in
person. All other material before the Tribunal was filed with
us at the hearing of this application.

The activities in the Middle East obviously have a
religious dimension. But to deny the political, social and
military realities when interpreting a word like "religious"
is to interpret a statute as would the judiciary in a
theocratic state. We are not concerned with the right or the
wrong of Mr. Forer's views but with whether the security of
geographic boundaries and the military activity with respect
thereto are matters religious and whether a religious
conviction in those regards are what s-s. 16(2) of the Act
contemplated.

Mr. Forer may be religiously inspired but in my respectful
view the recognition of the PLO as a legitimate
representative of the Palestinian people is not a matter of
religion per se. We must surely start with a "religious"
catalyst (if only in a most general and minimum objective
sense) before going on to the mind of the objector.
Otherwise, the most non-religious or a-religious
pronouncement or act of a trade union could provide grounds
for objection. We cannot accept that the legislator so
intended.

We prefer the approach of the Ontario Labour Relations
Board in Schochet v. OPSEU et al., [1983] O.L.R.B. Rep. 1472,
which is on all fours with the one at bar. The board refused
to accept, as the objector asserted, that "everything is
religious". We recognize that two different administrative
bodies can come to different and opposite conclusions on
essentially the same facts, both of which being beyond
judicial reach. Curial deference can take us that far. Not so
here, when the resolution of the issue turns on the manner of
defining the word "religious".
(Emphasis added.)

He concluded at p. 799 O.R., p. 612 D.L.R.:

In the result, the Tribunal erred in principle when
construing s-s. 16(2) of the Act. It cannot possibly or
reasonably be held to apply to the respondent here if it is
to have any meaning at all.

There was a misunderstanding about the submission made by Mr.
Forer in the Divisional Court. Smith J. in the passage quoted
above took him to say that "everything is religious". In his
dissent Saunders J. stated at p. 792 O.R., p. 605 D.L.R.:

I do not recall that he submitted to us that "everything is
religious" as apparently the applicant in the Humber College
case did.

In his submission to us, which was not objected to by counsel
for the respondent, Mr. Forer stated that he had never said
that "everything is religious". He suggested that this
quotation from the Humber College case [Schochet v. Ontario
Public Service Employees Union et al., [1983] O.L.R.B. Rep.
1472] might have been mistakenly attributed to him. Smith J.,
by italicizing this statement, which he believed Mr. Forer had
made, attached some importance to it but I do not consider that
his decision turned on it.

In his dissent Saunders J. disagreed with the majority's
characterization of Forer's views on the Middle East at p. 792
O.R., p. 605 D.L.R.:

The characterization of a belief or conviction as religious
must be subjective to a considerable degree ... Shortly
stated, it is his belief, which he founds on scripture, that
the Hebrew people have the exclusive right to occupy and
defend Israel against all comers. ... There are, no doubt,
many who would characterize his objection to the OFL
resolution as the political views of a religious man. Mr.
Forer did, however, make it clear that his view on the entire
situation in the Middle East was based on a source which he
considered to be divine. It is not for the Tribunal or this
court to decide on some a priori basis what beliefs are
capable of being religious in character.

The standard of review

In this Court the central issue was the effect of s. 39 of
the Act which reads as follows:

39. The Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to exercise the
powers conferred upon it by this Act and to determine all
questions of fact or law that arise in any matter before it,
and, except as otherwise provided in this Act, the action or
decision of the Tribunal thereon is final and binding for all
purposes, but nevertheless the Tribunal may at any time, if
it considers it advisable to do so, reconsider any decision,
order, direction, declaration or ruling made by it and vary
or revoke any such decision, order, direction, declaration or
ruling.
(Emphasis added.) Because of its importance I will deal with
this issue first and certain factual issues later.

A brief reference to well-settled rules of administrative law
will demonstrate the importance of determining whether the
section is a privative clause which protects the Tribunal's
decision from judicial review. The application for judicial
review in this case was made under s. 2(1) of the Judicial
Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 224. That section
empowers the court to grant any relief which would have been
available on, inter alia, an application for an order in the
nature of certiorari. In the absence of a privative clause, the
scope of review in certiorari proceedings includes questions of
both jurisdiction and law. If there is a privative clause, the
scope is limited to questions of jurisdiction.

If a tribunal acts within its jurisdiction under the
protection of a privative clause, it has what is commonly
called "the right to be wrong". Its decisions cannot be
attacked because they may be legally incorrect. In Teamsters
Union Local 938 et al. v. Massicotte et al.,
1982 CanLII 18 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R.
710 at p. 719, 134 D.L.R. (3d) 385 at p. 391, 82 C.L.L.C. para.

14
,196 (S.C.C.), Laskin C.J.C. stated:

... there can be no jurisdictional infirmity when the Board
is protected in its determinations by a privative clause. It
may be wrong in law in interpreting the range of powers
confided to it but its decisions are nonetheless immunized
from judicial review.

This principle was recently affirmed in this Court in Re United
Headwear, Optical & Allied Workers Union of Canada, Local 3 et
al. and Biltmore/Stetson (Canada) Inc. et al. (1983),
1983 CanLII 1802 (ON CA)
, 43 O.R.
(2d) 243 at p. 251, 150 D.L.R. (3d) 577 at pp. 584-5, per
Robins J.

A tribunal protected by a privative clause (after it has
properly embarked on its inquiry) can lose the protection of
that clause and hence its jurisdiction by committing errors in
the course of that inquiry. In Service Employees' Int'l Union,
Local No. 333 v. Nipawin District Staff Nurses Ass'n et al.,

1973 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 382 at p. 389, 41 D.L.R. (3d) 6 at pp. 11-2,
[1974] 1 W.W.R. 653, the Supreme Court of Canada held that
examples of such errors included:

... acting in bad faith, basing the decision on extraneous
matters, failing to take relevant factors into account,
breaching the provisions of natural justice or
misinterpreting provisions of the Act so as to embark on an
inquiry or answer a question not remitted to it.

In Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 963 v. New
Brunswick Liquor Corp.,
1979 CanLII 23 (SCC)
, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227, 97 D.L.R. (3d)
417, 25 N.B.R. (2d) 237 (S.C.C.) (the CUPE case), Dickson J.
dealt specifically with the effect of misinterpretation of the
governing statute as follows at p. 237 S.C.R. and p. 424
D.L.R.:

Did the Board here so misinterpret the provisions of the
Act as to embark on an inquiry or answer a question not
remitted to it? Put another way, was the Board's
interpretation so patently unreasonable that its construction
cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation
and demands intervention by the court upon review?
(Emphasis added.)

In this case, the standard of review of the Tribunal's
interpretation of the words "his religious convictions or
belief " in s. 16(2) depends on whether s. 39 has privative
effect. If the section has privative effect, the standard is
whether the Tribunal's interpretation of the words was
"patently unreasonable". If the section does not have
privative effect, the standard is whether the interpretation is
legally correct: see Board of Industrial Relations of Alberta
et al. v. Stedelbauer Chevrolet Oldsmobile Ltd.,
1968 CanLII 55 (SCC)
, [1969] S.C.R.
137, 1 D.L.R. (3d) 81, 65 W.W.R. 344.

Finality and "no certiorari" clauses

On a plain reading, s. 39 appears to preclude any review of
the Tribunal's decisions. The Tribunal has "exclusive
jurisdiction ... to determine all questions of fact or law ...
and ... the ... decision of the Tribunal ... is final and
binding for all pur- poses ... ". This, Mr. Brown submitted,
limited judicial review to questions of jurisdiction. Mr.
Cavalluzzo, on the contrary, contended that s. 39 did not have
this privative effect because it did not explicitly take away
the court's certiorari jurisdiction. Thus, in his submission,
the court was entitled to review questions of law as well as
jurisdiction.

He pointed out that other statutes protected the decisions of
administrative tribunals by two clauses rather than one as in
this Act. He described s. 39 as a "finality" clause which did
not have privative effect unless accompanied by a "no
certiorari" clause. He cited the Labour Relations Act, R.S.O.
1980, c. 228, as a typical example of a statute containing both
clauses. He described s. 106(1) of that Act, which is
substantially similar to s. 39 of the Act, as a "finality"
clause and s. 108 as a "no certiorari" clause. Section 108
provides:

108. No decision, order, direction, declaration or ruling
of the Board shall be questioned or reviewed in any court,
and no order shall be made or process entered, or proceedings
taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, declaratory
judgment, certiorari, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, or
otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the
Board or any of its proceedings.

He referred to Re Ontario Labour Relations Board, Bradley et
al. and Canadian General Electric Co. Ltd.,
1957 CanLII 114 (ON CA)
, [1957] O.R. 316, 8
D.L.R. (2d) 65, where Roach J.A. distinguished the two clauses.
In his judgment, Roach J.A. expressed the opinion that the
predecessor of the present s. 106 (a "finality" clause) did not
prevent certiorari proceedings but that they were precluded by
the predecessor of s. 108 (a "no certiorari" clause), which
Roach J.A. described as "a privative clause". He said at p. 332
O.R., p. 78 D.L.R.:

In his reasons Mr. Justice Wells referred to the judgment
of the Supreme Court of Canada in Labour Relations Board
(B.C.) and Attorney General for the Province of British
Columbia v. Canada Safeway Limited,
1953 CanLII 35 (SCC)
, [1953] 2 S.C.R. 46, 107
C.C.C. 75, [1953] 3 D.L.R. 641. Mr. Justice Wells saw no
difference between the Ontario Statute and the British
Columbia Act. The fact is that they differ in one most
important particular. In the Ontario Act there is a privitive
clause (s. 69) preventing certiorari proceedings; in the
British Columbia Act there was not. That distinction is most
important when we come to consider what was said in the
Canada Safeway case. Before dealing with what was said in
that case it is appropriate to consider the type of
legislation that is necessary to take away certiorari and to
point out that, though Parliament or the Legislature may by
adequate legislation take that remedy away for every other
purpose, it cannot take it away as a remedy where the
inferior tribunal has acted without or in excess of its
jurisdiction, because in such a case the inferior tribunal
has not brought itself within the terms of the statute taking
it away: Colonial Bank of Australasia v. Willan [(1874), L.R.
5 P.C. 417].

First, I point out that s. 2(4) of the British Columbia Act
was almost identical with s. 68(1) of the Ontario Act.
Neither of those sections, in my opinion, prevent certiorari.

Many statutes contain both "finality" and "no certiorari"
clauses. The latter are similar to s. 108, specifically
preventing the review of administrative decisions by certiorari
or other proceedings. The distinction between "finality" and
"no certiorari" clauses is referred to by textwriters. In
England, it appears to be accepted that a mere "finality"
clause unaccompanied by a ''no certiorari" clause does not have
privative effect: see de Smith, Judicial Review of
Administrative Action, 4th ed. (1980), pp. 364-9; Wade,
Administrative Law, 4th ed. (1977), pp. 566-77; Reid & David,
Administrative Law and Practice, 2nd ed. (1978), pp. 181-203;
Evans, Janisch, Mullan & Risk, Administrative Law Cases, Text,
and Materials, 2nd ed. (1984), pp. 531-5.

I am not persuaded that the English rule applies to Ontario
and that the omission of a "no certiorari" clause in the Act
deprives s. 39 of privative effect. The judgment of Roach J.A.
in the Bradley case is entitled to the greatest respect
because, as Estey J.A. pointed out in Douglas Aircraft Co. of
Canada Ltd. v. McConnell et al.,
1979 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 245 at p. 269,
99 D.L.R. (3d) 385 at p. 401, 79 C.L.L.C. para.
14
,221, it was
the "first comprehensive examination of the relationship
between court and board in labour law in our country". None the
less, his statement that a "no certiorari" clause was required
in addition to the "finality" clause must be regarded as obiter
because both types of clause appeared in the Labour Relations
Act of Ontario which he was then considering. In fact, I have
only been able to discover one decision of this Court holding
that a ''no certiorari" clause is required in addition to a
"finality" clause to bar review of a tribunal's decision on
questions of law and that decision was reversed by the Supreme
Court of Canada.

In Re Fraser and Pringle et al.,
1971 CanLII 35 (ON CA)
, [1971] 2 O.R. 749, 19 D.L.R.
(3d) 129, this Court dealt with an application for
certiorari to quash a deportation order. The Immigration Appeal
Board Act, 1966-67 (Can.), c. 90, gave a right of appeal from
deportation orders to the board. Under the previous procedure,
appeals against such orders could be made only to the Minister
who was empowered in his discretion to refer any appeal to the
Immigration Appeal Board. Although certiorari lay in respect of
deportation orders under the old procedure it was subject to a
privative clause which was deleted from the new statute.

Section 22 of the new Act vested in the board "sole and
exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all questions of
fact or law, including questions of jurisdiction, that may
arise in relation to the making of an order of deportation". In
the Fraser case, the applicant had appealed to the board
against a deportation order. Because of a backlog of cases, it
was admitted that his appeal could not be heard for at least
two years. The applicant applied by way of certiorari to quash
the deportation order because there were urgent personal and
humanitarian reasons for establishing his status speedily. His
application was rejected by the High Court on the ground that
s. 22 precluded it but, on appeal to this Court, the
deportation order was quashed. The Court held that this
section, which can be properly described as a "finality" clause
did not have privative effect because the right of certiorari
had not been expressly taken away by the statute. Arnup J.A.
said at pp. 760-1 O.R., pp. 140-1 D.L.R.:

I do not find in the Immigration Appeal Board Act any
language which clearly takes away this Court's jurisdiction
by way of certiorari, nor any language which could possibly
be said to transfer that jurisdiction to the Board or any
other Court.

In the Supreme Court of Canada, sub nom. Pringle et al. v.
Fraser,
1972 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, [1972] S.C.R. 821, 26 D.L.R. (3d) 28, Laskin J. held
that the s. 22 "finality" clause was sufficient to preclude
review. He stated at p. 828 S.C.R., p. 33 D.L.R., that the
addition of a "no certiorari" clause was not required because
it " ... would only make plainer what is already plain enough".

Pringle v. Fraser was obviously decided on its own special
facts. Laskin J. at p. 827 S.C.R., p. 32 D.L.R., held that the
new statutory right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board
was an exclusive remedy and incompatible with "the survival of
certiorari in the provincial courts". He said that for this
reason the legislation "cannot be tested by principles derived
from privative clauses". This case, therefore, may leave open
the question whether express language is required to take away
the right to certiorari. In my view, however, this decision
taken together with other decisions of the Supreme Court
indicates that no such requirement exists. Whether certiorari
is preserved by any statute depends on the proper construction
of "finality" or other preclusive clauses in the context of the
statute as a whole. This is illustrated by an earlier Supreme
Court of Canada decision which also gave privative effect to a
"finality" clause unsupported by a "no certiorari" clause.
In Labour Relations Board et al. v. Traders' Service Ltd.,

1958 CanLII 28 (SCC)
, [1958] S.C.R. 672 at p. 678, 15 D.L.R. (2d) 305 at p. 321,
Judson J. said:

By s. 65 of the Act the Board is required to determine
whether a person is an employer or employee and this decision
is to be final and conclusive. The matter, therefore, was
solely within the Board's jurisdiction and it is not open to
judicial review.

The evolving importance of "finality" clauses

More recent decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada indicate
a tendency to avoid the technical distinctions between errors
of law and jurisdiction. Where "finality" clauses appear in
statutes the court has followed the thrust of the CUPE decision
and refrained from interference with tribunal decisions for
which there is a "rational basis" or which are "not plainly
unreasonable". In doing so it has cut across the older
distinctions between law and jurisdiction.

In Syndicat des Employes de Production du Quebec et de
l'Acadie v. Canada Labour Relations Board et al.,
1984 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, [1984] 2
S.C.R. 412, 14 D.L.R. (4th) 457, 84 C.L.L.C. para.
14
,609, the
Supreme Court of Canada held that a "finality" clause similar
to s. 39 was sufficient to limit judicial review to a "rational
basis" standard, precluding review for error of law committed
by a tribunal while considering a matter within its
jurisdiction. It must be noted that this decision and others
dealing with federal tribunals come from the Federal Court of
Canada which has the statutory power to give relief in the
nature of certiorari but lacks the inherent jurisdiction of the
superior courts of the province to do so: see Federal Court
Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. 10 (2nd Supp.), ss. 18 and 28.
Nevertheless, the Supreme Court's decisions in these cases are
persuasive authority for limiting the scope of judicial review
of tribunal decisions protected by "finality" clauses and
narrowing, if not obliterating, the difference between the
standards of review applicable to questions of law and
jurisdiction.

The evolving attitude of the Supreme Court of Canada on this
issue is demonstrated by decisions in two cases dealing with
Alberta legislation, namely, Re Yellow Cab Ltd. v. Board of
Industrial Relations et al.,
1980 CanLII 228 (SCC)
, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 761, 114 D.L.R.
(3d) 427, 14 Alta. L.R. (2d) 39, and Re Alberta Union of
Provincial Employees et al. and Board of Governors of Olds
College,
1982 CanLII 186 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 923, 136 D.L.R. (3d) 1, [1983] 1
W.W.R. 593. Both decisions dealt with privative provisions in
Alberta statutes relating to labour relations. In the Yellow
Cab case the statute in question was the Alberta Labour Act,
1973 (Alta.), c. 33, and in the Olds College case, the Public
Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40. Both Acts
contained a "finality" clause similar to s. 39 followed by a
clause prohibiting review by way of injunction, declaratory
judgment, prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise and another
permitting review by way of certiorari or mandamus if
proceedings were undertaken within 30 days of the tribunal's
decision. In the Yellow Cab case the Supreme Court concluded
that the tribunal had erred in law and that its decision was
reviewable on a certiorari application filed within 30 days of
that decision. It rejected the argument that the "finality"
clause was tantamount to a privative clause making the
tribunal's decisions subject to attack only on grounds of
jurisdiction and it quashed the tribunal's decision.

A different result was reached in the Olds College case
decided only two years later. There the court also dealt with
an application made within the 30-day period for certiorari
based on an alleged error of law. The Olds decision does not
refer to the Yellow Cab case. It significantly modifies that
decision by holding that the right of review by way of
certiorari is limited by the effect of the "finality" clauses
in the governing statute which were similar to the statutory
provisions in the Yellow Cab case. The court held that, where
the tribunal's interpretation of the statute was challenged as
erroneous in law, a court should not interfere with that
interpretation unless it was "plainly unreasonable". Laskin
C.J.C. put the matter this way at p. 927 S.C.R., p. 4 D.L.R.:

It will be noted that ... certiorari or mandamus ... remain
as procedural resorts to challenge decisions of the Board ...
In the face of this explicit provision for review, it is
impossible to read it out of this statute or to subordinate
it to ss. 9 [a "finality" clause limited to specific tribunal
decisions] and 11 [a "finality" clause similar to s. 39] or
even to limit it to questions of jurisdiction in the strict
sense, as urged by counsel for the Union and counsel for the
Board. That being said, however, it still remains to consider
the scope of review on alleged errors of law, and it is my
opinion that the commanding terms of s. 9(1) and especially
of s. 11 cast a gloss on the extent to which decisions of the
Board may be overturned by a Court. Certiorari, considered in
the light of ss. 9(1) and 11, is a long way from an appeal
and is subject to restriction in accordance with a line of
decisions of this Court which, to assess them generally,
preclude judicial interference with interpretations made by
the Board which are not plainly unreasonable.
(Emphasis added.)

The Olds College decision has been interpreted by one Alberta
judge as altering the standard of review. In Re Northside
Electric Ltd. and Int'l Brotherhood of Electrical Workers,
Local Union 424 et al. (1983),
1983 CanLII 1135 (AB QB)
, 4 D.L.R. (4th) 635, 30 Alta.
L.R. (2d) 173, 53 A.R. 114, Miller J. had this to say at p.
643:

The law on the standard for judicial review was altered in
the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Re Alberta
Union of Provincial Employees et al. and Board of Governors
of Olds College (1982),
1982 CanLII 186 (SCC)
, 136 D.L.R. (3d) 1, [1982] 1 S.C.R.
923, 37 A.R. 281. In that case, the Supreme Court adopted the
notion of "curial deference"; that is, when a board makes an
interpretation of its constituent Act, the court ought to be
loath to overturn that decision. In these circumstances, the
standard for review is as follows [at p. 7 D.L.R., p. 289
A.R., per Laskin C.J.C., quoting from Dickson J. in Canadian
Union of Public Employees, Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor
Corp. (1979),
1979 CanLII 23 (SCC)
, 97 D.L.R. (3d) 417 at p. 25 [sic], [1979] 2
S.C.R. 227, 25 N.B.R. (2d) 237]:

" ... was the Board's interpretation so patently
unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally
supported by the relevant legislation and demands
intervention by the court upon review?"

The Alberta Court of Appeal has had opportunity to discuss
this issue in light of the decision in Olds College. In Re
Suncor Inc. and McMurray Independent Oil Workers Local #1
(1982),
1982 ABCA 343 (CanLII)
, 142 D.L.R. (3d) 305, 23 Alta. L.R. (2d) 105,
[1982] 1 W.W.R. 604, the court held that so long as: (a)
the Board addressed itself to the issue it was charged to
address, and nothing more; (b) there was no failure of
natural justice; and (c) the Board was interpreting its
constituent statute, then even if the Board erred in law, it
was immunized from judicial review. In United Nurses of
Alberta, Local 11 et al. v. Misericordia Hospital (1983),
1983 ABCA 188 (CanLII)
, 27
Alta. L.R. (2d) 71, 46 A.R. 172, [1983] 6 W.W.R. 1, the Court
of Appeal affirmed the decision in Suncor. Stevenson J.A.,
for the majority, reviewed the argument that the scope of
judicial review set out in Suncor and Olds College applies
only to errors of law on the face of the record and not to
errors going to jurisdiction. Stevenson J.A. stated at p.
174: "That distinction is not easily drawn and I see a
tendency to reject it in favour of other formulations."

In this manner, Stevenson J.A. rejects the classification
of errors which was required prior to the decisions in Olds
College and Suncor in favour of the type of tests set out in
Suncor and attacks on a board's decision for jurisdictional
errors are considerably narrowed.

Changing judicial attitude to judicial review

These recent decisions of the Supreme Court reflect the
marked change in the attitude of courts towards decisions of
administrative tribunals which has occurred in recent years.
The story of what Estey J. has euphemistically described as "a
thinly disguised sense of rivalry between the traditional
courts and the statutory tribunals" in the Douglas case at p.
269 S.C.R. and p. 400 D.L.R. is well known and need only be
referred to briefly.

Administrative law remained relatively undeveloped in Canada
until after the Second World War. It was based on judicial
decisions and reflected attitudes which emerged in England
earlier in this century when boards and tribunals began to
proliferate as instruments of governmental social policy and
economic control. The English courts confined the power of
boards and tribunals within the strictest limits and resisted
legislative attempts to immunize their decisions from judicial
interference. The distinction made between "finality" and "no
certiorari" clauses is an example of this judicial attitude.

In the immediate post-war years, these attitudes were
reflected in the decisions of Canadian courts. Most provinces
enacted legislation which protected the decisions of tribunals
with both "finality" and "no certiorari" clauses. While courts
acknowledged that these provisions limited the scope of
judicial interference to questions of jurisdiction, many
tribunal decisions were struck down as judges avidly searched
for jurisdictional error in circumstances where it could not be
established today. The era of judicial activism in
administrative law has ended and many decisions from that time,
although never specifically overruled, must now be considered
to have little or no effect. The sad tale of this strife
between courts and boards was recorded by Professor Bora Laskin
(as he then was), in "Certiorari to Labour Boards: The
Apparent Futility of Privative Clauses", 30 Can. Bar Rev. 986
(1952); see also H. Sutherland, "Administrative Law
-- Privative Clauses and the Courts -- A Review", ibid. p. 69,
and P.J. Millward, "Judicial Review of Administrative
Authorities in Canada", 39 Can. Bar Rev. 351 (1961).

The judicial attitude to tribunals has changed. Restraint has
replaced intervention as judicial policy. Courts now recognize
the legitimate role of administrative tribunals in the
development and execution of economic, social and political
policies ordained by the Legislature. Judges also recognize
that tribunals bring to bear in their decisions knowledge and
expertise in their particular fields beyond the usual
experience of the courts. The new judicial attitude towards
tribunals is sometimes described as "curial deference" and is
epitomized by a passage from the judgment of Chief Justice
Laskin in Canada Labour Relations Board et al. v. Halifax
Longshoremen's Ass'n et al.,
1983 CanLII 133 (SCC)
, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 245 at p. 256, 144
D.L.R. (3d) 1 at p. 8, 83 C.L.L.C. para.
14
,022, where he said:

It is rarely a simple matter to draw a line between a
lawful and unlawful exercise of power by a statutory
tribunal, however ample its authority, when there are
conflicting considerations addressed to the exercise of
power. This Court has, over quite a number of years, thought
it more consonant with the legislative objectives involved in
a case such as this to be more rather than less deferential
to the discharge of difficult tasks by statutory tribunals
like the Board.

A more detailed exposition of the current judicial attitude
towards administrative tribunals was given by Dickson J. in the
CUPE case, supra, at pp. 235-6 S.C.R., p. 424 D.L.R.:

The rationale for protection of a labour board's decisions
within jurisdiction is straightforward and compelling. The
labour board is a specialized tribunal which administers a
comprehensive statute regulating labour relations. In the
administration of that regime, a board is called upon not
only to find facts and decide questions of law, but also to
exercise its understanding of the body of jurisprudence that
has developed around the collective bargaining system, as
understood in Canada, and its labour relations sense acquired
from accumulated experience in the area.

The usual reasons for judicial restraint upon review of
labour board decisions are only reinforced in a case such as
the one at bar. Not only has the Legislature confided certain
decisions to the administrative board, but to a separate and
distinct Public Service Labour Relations Board. That Board is
given broad powers -- broader than those typically vested in
a labour board -- to supervise and administer the novel
system of collective bargaining created by the Public Service
Labour Relations Act. The Act calls for a delicate balance
between the need to maintain public services, and the need to
maintain collective bargaining. Considerable sensitivity and
unique expertise on the part of Board members is all the more
required if the twin purposes of the legislation are to be
met. Nowhere is the application of those skills more evident
than in the supervision of a lawful strike by public service
employees under the Act. Although the New Brunswick Act is
patterned closely upon the
federal Public Service Staff
Relations Act
, 1966-67 (Can.), c. 72, section 102(3) is not
found in the federal legislation nor, in fact, in any other
public sector labour legislation in Canada. The
interpretation of s. 102(3) would seem to lie logically at
the heart of the specialized jurisdiction confided to the
Board. In that case, not only would the Board not be required
to be "correct" in its interpretation, but one would think
that the Board was entitled to err and any such error would
be protected from review by the privative clause in s. 101.

These passages were quoted with approval by Robins J.A.
speaking for this Court in the United Headware Union case,
supra, where he said at p. 251 O.R., pp. 584-5 D.L.R.:

Whether a particular error can be characterized as
"jurisdictional" and hence outside the protection of the
privative clause is, as the cases amply demonstrate, often
very difficult to determine, and the courts have been
admonished not to be alert to brand as jurisdictional, and
therefore subject to broader curial review, that which may be
doubtfully so.

The new judicial attitude has also been exemplified by
decisions in the Divisional Court. In Re Tandy Electronics Ltd.
and United Steelworkers of America et al. (1980),
1980 CanLII 1738 (ON HCJ)
, 30 O.R. (2d)
29 at p. 42, 115 D.L.R. (3d) 197 at p. 210, 80 C.L.L.C. para.

14
,017, Cory J. referred to the CUPE case, supra, and said:

No matter what is the particular wording used in the
decisions, the message is clear -- a cautious approach must
be taken by the Courts when considering whether a tribunal
has lost jurisdiction as a result of something it did during
the course of a hearing. The Board may well make a mistake.
Unless that mistake is patently unreasonable, or so
fundamentally erroneous, that it cries aloud for intervention
by the reviewing Court, it should not constitute a ground for
depriving the Board of the protection of the privative
clause.

In Re Int'l Union of Operating Engineers, Local 793 and
Traugott Construction Ltd. (1984),
1984 CanLII 2011 (ON HCJ)
, 45 O.R. (2d) 129 at p. 137,
6 D.L.R. (4th) 122 at p. 131, 84 C.L.L.C. para.
14
,025, Osler
J. said:

What fell from Dickson J., then [in the CUPE case] can now be
regarded as the new foundation of this branch of
administrative law and renders it unnecessary any longer in
these cases to indulge in the type of casuistic reasoning so
frequently found in the earlier cases.

The effect of procedural reform

In this province, the new attitudes have achieved greater
prominence because of the rationalization and the
institutionalization of the procedure for judicial review
resulting from the passage of the Judicial Review Procedure Act
in 1971 (Ont.), c. 48, now R.S.O. 1980, c. 224. This Act gave
legislative recognition to the importance of administrative
tribunals and, at the same time, made their regulation and
control an ordinary incident rather than an extraordinary
feature of the work of the courts. The rules applicable to
judicial review of tribunal decisions by the prerogative writs
have been preserved by this statute but the manner in which
they are employed has been altered by their new institutional
setting. Procedure for judicial review has been simplified and
technicalities virtually eliminated. A broad body of
jurisprudence has been established governing judicial review as
a recognized and established function of the courts in today's
complex society.

The factors at work in the evolution of administrative law
are relevant to the interpretation of s. 39. Courts now
recognize the legitimacy of tribunals as an essential part of
the structure of government and the legal system. They respect
both the status conferred on tribunals by the Legislature and
their expertise in the performance of the tasks assigned to
them. It is a natural consequence of this new attitude that
courts now respect the intention of Legislatures to limit
judicial review and statutory provisions clearly expressing
that intent. It would not be consonant with the present state
of the law to fasten upon s. 39 the requirement that it be
accompanied by a "no certiorari" clause in order to give it the
privative effect obviously intended by the Legislature.

It also would be almost absurd to force such a restrictive
interpretation on s. 39 for the reasons which have been
advanced for restricting similar so-called "finality" clauses
in the past. At pp. 366-7, de Smith states that a bare
"finality" clause, not supported by a "no certiorari"
clause, merely takes away a right of appeal, if one already
exists, and precludes a tribunal from rescinding or rectifying
its own decisions: see also R. v. Medical Appeal Tribunal, Ex
p. Gilmore,
[1957] 1 Q.B. 574, [1957] 1 All E.R. 796 (C.A.)
,
per Parker L.J. at p. 589.

Assuming the legal omniscience which courts attribute to the
Legislature, one might ask why s. 39 would be enacted if these
were its only purposes. Decisions of the Tribunal are not
appealable. Under s. 39, the Tribunal has power to rescind or
alter its previous decisions. If s. 39 was a mere "finality"
clause, in the sense described in de Smith, it would serve no
purpose. Such a conclusion would violate the basic canon of
statutory construction that the Legislature must be presumed to
intend that effect should be given to every provision in a
statute. That intended effect is clearly that the Tribunal,
acting within the jurisdiction conferred upon it, should be
permitted to perform its important functions free from judicial
interference.

I have, therefore, concluded that s. 39 should be given
privative effect. The consequence is that the appropriate
standard of review of the Tribunal's interpretation of the
words "religious convictions or belief " is whether it is or is
not patently unreasonable.

Implications of the CUPE decision

For the purpose of this decision it has sufficed to find that
no reason can be found in the Act or the decided cases for
requiring a ''no certiorari" clause before privative effect
will be given to the "finality" clause. It has thus been
possible to dispose of the issue on the traditional doctrinal
basis of differentiating between questions of law and
jurisdiction. There is, however, a growing body of opinion that
the decisions in CUPE and the cases stemming from it have
blurred, if not obliterated, the differences between questions
of law and jurisdiction. The tests of "patent unreasonableness"
or its reciprocal, a "rational basis" for the interpretation of
the governing statute, cut across the issues of law and
jurisdiction. In my opinion, Evans, Janisch, Mullan and Risk
are correct in concluding at p. 512:

An important aspect of the reasoning in CUPE is that it
relates jurisdictional review to the seriousness of the
agency's error rather than to the nature of the question it
had to decide.

The consequences of these decisions remain to be developed in
future cases. In Re Hughes Boat Works Inc. and Int'l Union,
United Automobile, Aerospace, Agricultural & Implement Workers
of America (UAW) Local 1620 et al. (1979),
1979 CanLII 1853 (ON HCJ)
, 26 O.R. (2d) 420 at
p. 428, 102 D.L.R. (3d) 661 at pp. 668-9, 79 C.L.L.C. para.

15
,361, Reid J. said:

I would thus prefer that the subjective nature of the
process be acknowledged and that we attempt to state the
considerations that should be borne in mind. Thus, rather
than simply categorizing elements in the decisions of
tribunals as jurisdictional or otherwise, I think we should
try to illustrate what will lead a Court to interfere or to
refrain from interfering with what a tribunal has done or
decided notwithstanding a privative clause.

It seems to me that below the veneer of the traditional
discussion about whether there exists an error of
jurisdiction or one "merely" of law there are two matters of
constant and unchanging concern. The first is whether there
is a genuine error of law. The second is whether it is of
such magnitude that it requires an interference by the Court
in the administrative process in light of the desirability of
refraining from interference as much as possible.

I think that what may transmute an error of law in our
minds into one of jurisdiction is frequently little more than
the conviction that the error is a serious one justifying an
intervention.

With these thoughts in mind I make bold to suggest what is
the appropriate question to ask oneself when facing a
privative clause. I think it is this: is there here an error
of law and if so, is it of such magnitude as to require
intervention in light of the general principle that Courts
should intervene in the administrative process as little as
possible?

Looking at the questions before us in this light requires
looking past the privative clause to see what the Board
decided.

In Re Tandy Electronics and United Steelworkers of America,
Cory J. expressed approval for Reid's test in the Hughes Boat
case and at p. 42 O.R., p. 210 D.L.R., formulated the question
the court should ask itself as ''whether there was an error of
law of such magnitude that it should intervene". This, in his
view, was another way of expressing the test of Dickson J. in
CUPE that a tribunal's decision must be "so patently
unreasonable that it demanded intervention of the court upon
review". These decisions point to a compromise between
questions of law and jurisdiction which could render the
distinction between "finality" and "no certiorari" clauses
completely academic. In my opinion this realistic and
functional approach to the review of decisions of
administrative tribunals is now open to the courts and should
be applied in such cases as this.

The preliminary or collateral issue

The alternative argument of the appellant was that the
Tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction in commencing its inquiry.
Mr. Cavalluzzo contended that the Tribunal had to make two
separate decisions in determining whether Mr. Forer was
entitled to exemption from paying union dues because of "his
religious convictions or belief ". First, it was required to
decide as a matter of law what the phrase "religious
convictions and belief " meant. Then it had to apply that
definition to the facts. He argued that the first determination
was preliminary or collateral, in the language employed by the
cases, and had to be made before the Tribunal exercised its
jurisdiction to decide whether Forer was entitled to the
exemption. Since it was collateral it was outside the
jurisdiction of the Tribunal and was, therefore, reviewable,
unprotected by the privative clause.

This is not a case where issues of law and fact should or can
be segregated in the decision-making process. The Tribunal, in
order to determine whether an applicant is entitled to
exemption on the grounds of "his religious convictions or
belief ", must decide both as a question of law what the phrase
means and as a question of fact whether the applicant is
covered by its interpretation of the phrase. These two
decisions are intertwined and are clearly confided to the
jurisdiction of the Tribunal. It would be artificial to the
point of sophistry to attempt to separate them. The
interpretation and application of the language of the statute
lies, in the words of Dickson J. in CUPE at p. 236 S.C.R., p.
424 D.L.R., "logically at the heart of the specialized
jurisdiction confided to the Board". The Tribunal under s. 39
has exclusive jurisdiction to determine "all questions of fact
or law that arise in any matter before it" and it would fly in
the face of the statute to divide these questions.

A similar argument was raised in the CUPE case where it was
asserted that as a preliminary to the making of its decision
the administrative tribunal had to interpret the relevant
provisions of the governing statute. Dickson J. rejected the
contention that the decision of the tribunal at issue in that
case could be divided and at p. 233 S.C.R., p. 421 D.L.R. made
the following observations:

With respect, I do not think that the language of
"preliminary or collateral matter" assists in the inquiry
into the Board's jurisdiction. One can, I suppose, in most
circumstances subdivide the matter before an administrative
tribunal into a series of tasks or questions and, without too
much difficulty, characterize one of those questions as a
"preliminary or collateral matter". As Wade suggests in
his Administrative Law ... questions of fact will naturally
be regarded as "the primary and central questions for
decision", whereas the "prescribed statutory ingredients will
more readily be found to be collateral". This is precisely
what has occurred in this case, the existence of the
prohibition described in the statute becoming the "collateral
matter", and the facts possibly constituting breach of the
prohibition, however interpreted, the "primary matter for
enquiry".

Dickson J. held at p. 237 S.C.R. and pp. 424-5 D.L.R. that
the Board had decided "a matter which was plainly confided to
it, for it alone to decide within its jurisdiction" and that it
had "jurisdiction in the narrow sense of authority to enter
upon an inquiry". His reasons govern this case where the
decision of mixed law and fact is similar to that in the CUPE
case. In my opinion, his judgment has greatly reduced the
significance of the doctrine of the preliminary or collateral
question in Canadian administrative law.

Did the tribunal's decision meet the standard of review?

In my opinion, the Tribunal correctly applied the proper
standard of review in this case. It cannot be said that its
interpretation of s. 16(2) was patently unreasonable when it
held that Forer was entitled to exemption from paying dues to
OPSEU "because of his religious convictions and belief ".

In the passage quoted from the Van Harten decision, supra,
the Tribunal enumerated the factors to be considered in the
application of the section. They can be briefly summarized. The
words "his religious convictions and belief " must be
considered from the subjective point of view of the applicant.
The Tribunal must be convinced that the applicant's views are
sincerely held as religious convictions in order to ensure that
they are not advanced as a subterfuge to escape the payment of
dues. The Tribunal cannot impose its own or any other a priori
view of what is "religious" on the applicant. The word
"religious" does not require that the individual's beliefs
must be the tenets of any religious denomination. Only in rare
cases will it be necessary to test an applicant's convictions
against some objective definition of the word "religious".

The majority of the Divisional Court accepted the Tribunal's
criteria with one exception. While agreeing with the Tribunal's
view that "religion is subjective and personal to the person",
Smith J. stated that religious convictions must be subjected to
an objective test. In his view, the opinions of Mr. Forer were
not "religious" but were political and even war-like against
the P.L.O. The lessons of history, unhappily, show that this,
in itself, is no reason for concluding that his convictions are
not religiously based. This is especially true in the Middle
East, a region where extreme political views and violence are
often justified on religious grounds. The task of the Tribunal,
therefore, was not to pass judgment on the quality of Forer's
religious beliefs but rather to determine if they could be
accepted as religious beliefs whatever their consequences or
however expressed. It is the Court's duty to determine whether
or not the Tribunal's conclusion that these were religious
convictions and beliefs within the meaning of s. 16(2) was
patently unreasonable. It is not the function of the Court on
review to attempt a precise definition of the words "religious
convictions or belief ". Even if the reviewing court might have
reached a different result, it cannot interfere with the
Tribunal's decision unless it is held to be "patently
unreasonable".

Some assistance is, however, provided by discussions of the
meaning of "religion" or "religious beliefs" in other cases.
Two decisions of this Court stress the variety of religions and
religious practices in Canada and the fact that what may be
regarded as a religious belief or practice by one religion may
be regarded as secular by another. This is illustrated by the
following passage from the judgment of Tarnopolsky J.A. in R.
v. Videoflicks Ltd. (1984),
1984 CanLII 44 (ON CA)
, 48 O.R. (2d) 395 at pp. 420-2, 14
D.L.R. (4th) 10 at pp. 35-7, 15 C.C.C. (3d) 353:

What follows is in no way to be taken as an exhaustive
definition of the fundamental freedom of religion embodied in
s. 2(a) of the Charter. ... Freedom of religion goes beyond
the ability to hold certain beliefs without coercion and
restraint and entails more than the ability to profess those
beliefs openly. In my view, freedom of religion also includes
the right to observe the essential practices demanded by the
tenets of one's religion and, in determining what those
essential practices are in any given case, the analysis must
proceed not from the majority's perspective of the concept of
religion but in terms of the role that the practices and
beliefs assume in the religion of the individual or group
concerned.

. . . . .

... all religions require their adherents to observe the
tenets of that religion by various practices which would
appear to others to have a purely secular significance, such
as not cutting one's hair and wearing turbans, or shaving
one's head and wearing saffron robes, such as not eating
certain foods or eating them on certain days and not others,
such as not killing certain animals or consuming some and not
others and, above all, such as not working or buying or
selling goods or services on certain days specified as the
sabbath. Such observations, when practised as part of a
religious observance, have to be considered within the scope
of one's religious freedom. This is so even though what is a
religious practice for people of one religion is secular for
those of another and vice versa.

A similar view was expressed in this Court's decision in
Donald et al. v. Board of Education for City of Hamilton et
al.,
1945 CanLII 117 (ON CA)
, [1945] O.R. 518, [1945] 3 D.L.R. 424. There the Court set
aside the expulsion of pupils affiliated with the Jehovah's
Witnesses who had refused, on religious grounds, to participate
in school ceremonies involving saluting the flag and singing
the national anthem. The question before the Court was whether
these activities were "religious exercises" from which pupils
were entitled to be exempted by statute and regulation. The
Court rejected the argument that the exercises could not
reasonably be said to have any religious significance and
Gillanders J.A. stated at pp. 528-9 O.R., pp. 428-9 D.L.R.:

If I were permitted to be guided by my personal views, I
would find it difficult to understand how any well-disposed
person could offer objection to joining in such a salute on
religious or other grounds.

. . . . .

But ... it would be misleading to proceed on any personal
views on what such exercises might include or exclude.

The recent decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321,
18 C.C.C. (3d) 385, recognized the diversity of religions and
religious practices in Canada. In his discussion of the
guarantee of "freedom of conscience and religion" which is
entrenched in
s. 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
, Chief Justice Dickson said at p. 351 S.C.R., p. 365
D.L.R.:

In an earlier time, when people believed in the collective
responsibility of the community toward some deity, the
enforcement of religious conformity may have been a
legitimate object of government, but since the
Charter
, it is
no longer legitimate. With the Charter, it has become the
right of every Canadian to work out for himself or herself
what his or her religious obligations, if any, should be and
it is not for the state to dictate otherwise.

It seems to me that in the multicultural country which Canada
has become there will have to be even greater toleration of a
wide variety of religious beliefs and practices than existed
before the
Charter
. Certainly, for the purposes of s. 16(2) of
the Act, views cannot be described as "non-religious" because
they differ from the religious beliefs of the dominant groups
in society.

As I observed previously, it is unnecessary for the purpose
of this case to attempt any comprehensive definition of the
words "religion" or "religious". It suffices to say that there
was evidence to support the view that Mr. Forer's views were
"religious" as Saunders J. explained in the following
passage at p. 793 O.R., p. 607 D.L.R.:

In Butler v. York University Faculty Ass'n et al., [1981]
O.L.R.B. Rep. 1319, at p. 1328, para. 17, it was said for
beliefs or convictions to be characterized as "religious",
that:

" ... the beliefs must relate to the Divine (in some form)
and man's perceived relationship to the Divine, rather than
to concepts which deal only with man-made institutions and
the relationship of man inter se."

It is noted that in his application for an exemption, Mr.
Forer stated that the recent resolution of the OFL "is
inimical to every Jew who believes in the God given right to
the land of Israel".

Having regard to the criteria established by the Tribunal, I
agree with the conclusion of Saunders J. at p. 793 O.R., p. 607
D.L.R. that:

... it was not unreasonable for the Tribunal to have
concluded that the objection of Mr. Forer to the resolution
was founded on a religious belief. There was evidence to
support such a conclusion and we should not interfere with
it.

The factual issues

In order to avoid confusion with the main question of the
interpretation and application of s. 39, I deferred reference
to two factual issues on which the majority in the Divisional
Court disagreed with the Tribunal. The first issue arises from
the fact that the resolution, against which Mr. Forer
complains, was not passed by OPSEU, the union to which his dues
were paid, but by the OFL, a federation of unions of which
OPSEU was only one member. The argument was that OPSEU itself
had done nothing to justify an objection under s. 16(2). The
majority in the Divisional Court accepted this argument and
held that the OFL resolution was too "remote" to provide a
valid ground for objection by a member of OPSEU.

The second issue is whether, at the time of the hearing by
the Tribunal, there was any Middle East policy in existence to
which Mr. Forer could object. It will be recalled that, under
its constitution, the OFL could only recommend foreign policy
resolutions for adoption by the CLC. The material placed before
the Tribunal by OPSEU included a letter from the CLC to the OFL
which reported that the resolution had been discussed at a
meeting of the CLC executive council and that it had been
decided "to reiterate the position of the CLC on the Middle
East". After the Tribunal's decision an affidavit was filed
with the Divisional Court stating that the effect of the CLC's
action was to reject the resolution of the OFL. The majority in
the Divisional Court held that the OFL resolution was "spent"
because it could have no effect unless accepted by the CLC.

Saunders J. dissented holding that there was some evidence
before the Tribunal which would support its decision on both
issues. I agree with him that such evidence exists. The fact of
its existence precludes any interference with the Tribunal's
decision.

In view of this conclusion, it is not necessary to decide
whether the affidavit adding to the record placed before the
Tribunal should have been admitted by the Divisional Court.
This Court has held that such affidavits are admissible in the
Divisional Court only to show there was no evidence before a
tribunal to support its findings and not merely to provide
additional evidence: Re Keeprite Workers' Independent Union et
al. and Keeprite Products Ltd. (1980),
1980 CanLII 1877 (ON CA)
, 29 O.R. (2d) 513, 114
D.L.R. (3d) 162; Re Securicor Investigations & Security Ltd.
and Ontario Labour Relations Board et al. (1985),
1985 CanLII 1978 (ON HCJ)
, 50 O.R. (2d)
570, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 151. In any event, the question whether
the action of the CLC constituted rejection of the OFL
resolution has little significance. Mr. Forer also objected on
religious grounds to the CLC policy statement on the Middle
East because it supported the creation of a homeland for
Palestinians in the State of Israel.

For the foregoing reasons I would allow the appeal and direct
that the order of the Divisional Court be set aside. There
should be no order as to costs of this appeal.

Appeal allowed.
